changes.title: Men and money
changes.briefing: Your opinion went up to Her Majesty on the evening of the 26th, by your own hand and not the President's: men and money for Silesia now, raised on credit under her signature. She read it overnight and had Starhemberg with her when she saw you on the 27th. She will borrow, but wants the terms and the regiments named before the Conference sits on Monday. The bankers will lend short and dear; Starhemberg would rather wait for the Estates; Bartenstein points to the guarantor courts. President Harrach has your draft orders to the regiments on his table and has not signed them.

reports.source: your wife, left on your writing table
reports.title: Unless it is necessary
reports.text: You were kind last night and I believed you, so do not spoil it by reading this as a scold. But you said 'unless it is necessary', and I have lived with soldiers long enough to know that from now until the peace it will always be necessary. So I will not count dinners. I will count Sundays: give me those, and the girls will have their father one day in seven. Maria Antonia asks whether the Queen is pretty. I said she is tired. The tailor sent his boy round again; the steward says he has your answer for him. P.

guidance.known: Your wife takes your promise and asks for one day in seven instead of every dinner.
guidance.stakes: A small promise kept at home is easier than a large one broken; the tailor is still unpaid and still talking.

reports.title: Your opinion, the President and the antechambers
reports.text: Fact: Your Excellency's opinion on Silesia, fair-copied in my hand and signed by you, was carried to Her Majesty's apartments at seven in the evening of the 26th and given into the hand of her chamber servant, sealed. Fact: a copy went to President Harrach at nine on the 27th, with your compliments and the words 'for his information, Her Majesty having commanded the opinion of the Vice-President in person'. Fact: the draft orders to the regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary, that they fill their ranks, draw their arrears as far as the money allows and stand ready to march on further orders, went to the Hofkriegsrat chancery on the 26th for signature as the forms require. They are still there. Report: the President and Count Sinzendorf were together an hour at the Chancery on the 25th; their servants waited in the yard. Fact: on your order I sounded, without committing Your Excellency, one of the banking houses of the town on what it would lend against Her Majesty's signature; its answer is enclosed separately. Rumour, from a clerk in the Hofkammer: Count Starhemberg was asked by Her Majesty on the 26th how much the Banco could find in a month, and answered 'nothing that is not already promised'.

guidance.known: The opinion reached Her Majesty on the 26th; the President had his copy on the 27th, after it went up. The regimental orders wait for his signature.
guidance.suspected: Harrach and Sinzendorf met the day before the opinion went up; they may have agreed how to receive it.
guidance.stakes: You have kept your word to Her Majesty and given the President cause to remember the form of it.
guidance.explain: Orders of the Hofkriegsrat to the regiments go out under the President's signature or by the sovereign's own resolution. A Vice-President drafts; he does not command the army alone.

reports.source: Count Starhemberg, in his own hand
reports.title: On credit
reports.text: Count. I hear you ask for men and money. Good: someone should ask for both at once. Here is what money there is. The Banco cannot lend what it has not received. Its receipts for the year are assigned. It can advance against the Lower Austrian Estates' grant once the homage is done and the Estates have voted; that is weeks, not days, and the Estates will name their price. Bankers will lend tomorrow on the Queen's signature, at a high rate and for a short term, and they will want a revenue named. Every revenue you name to them is one you cannot name to the Estates. Do not pledge Silesia's contribution; a banker discounts a province that may be lost, and he will tell the town why. I will put this to Her Majesty plainly if she asks me. She has. Starhemberg.

guidance.known: The Banco's receipts are assigned; it can advance only after the Estates vote. Bankers lend at once, dear and short, against a named revenue.
guidance.suspected: Starhemberg prefers the slower road because it keeps the Banco in charge of the money.
guidance.stakes: Whichever revenue is pledged first cannot be pledged again.
guidance.explain: A loan from a banking house is liquid money now and an obligation that falls due in months, usually before the next grant is collected.

reports.source: Johann Georg Lenz, banker in the Wollzeile, to your secretary
reports.title: An answer in confidence
reports.text: Sir. I answer your question as it was put, as a question. My house and two others of the town could find among us two to three hundred thousand florins within the fortnight, in coin and in good bills on Amsterdam, if Her Majesty's own signature stands on the bond and a revenue is named that our agents can see collected: the Bohemian contribution, or the tobacco, or the salt. Not under eight in the hundred; six months, renewable at our discretion. We should want it known to no one until the bond is signed. If the news from the north should turn bad before then, the terms will turn with it. That is not a threat, sir; it is Amsterdam. Your servant, Lenz.

guidance.known: Two to three hundred thousand florins within a fortnight, at eight in the hundred or more, for six months, against Her Majesty's signature and a named revenue.
guidance.suspected: 'Two others of the town' may mean the houses already lending to the Hofkammer; the same money could be counted twice.
guidance.stakes: Enough to pay the Silesian garrisons and begin the works, not to raise an army. Bad news from Berlin would raise the price.
guidance.explain: Bills on Amsterdam are as good as coin to a paymaster who must buy abroad, and worth little to a regiment that wants bread in Silesia.

reports.title: The orders on my table
reports.asks: Do you leave your orders to the regiments with the President to sign in his time, or ask Her Majesty to resolve them herself?
reports.text: My dear Count. I thank you for the copy of your opinion. It reached me after it reached Her Majesty, which I am sure was the hour's fault and not yours. I find in my chancery also certain orders to the regiments in your hand, that they fill their ranks and stand ready to march. Orders to march are a resolution of the Council, and the Council has not met on them. The Conference fixed no money; a regiment told to stand ready and not paid will stand ready to desert. I shall lay them before the Council at its next sitting, with your opinion, and with my own. If Her Majesty prefers to resolve the matter herself, she has only to say so, and I shall sign whatever she has signed. Harrach.

guidance.known: The President will not sign until the Council has sat, and says so in writing.
guidance.suspected: He has agreed his line with Count Sinzendorf; the Council will hear the case for waiting before it hears yours.
guidance.stakes: If you go to Her Majesty over his head a second time, he will not forgive it; if you do not, the regiments do not move this month.
guidance.explain: A sovereign's resolution overrides the Council; it is also remembered by every minister who sees it used against a President of three reigns.

reports.title: On the guarantors
reports.text: Your Excellency. I have had the honour of reading, at Her Majesty's command, your opinion, and I agree with its conclusion and with very little of its reasoning, which is the usual condition of agreement in this house. You ask for money from our allies. The Crown of Great Britain guaranteed the Sanction by the treaty of 16 March 1731, the States General afterwards by their own act; a guarantee that is never called upon is a compliment. I would call upon it, through the Chancery, which is the only door to London that does not lead to a counting-house. I would not let the Chancery's slowness be an argument for not knocking. If Your Excellency would say as much in Conference on Monday, I should say the rest. Bartenstein.

guidance.known: Bartenstein supports men and money and offers to carry the appeal to the guarantor courts in Conference with you.
guidance.suspected: He wants the credit for the treaties, and Sinzendorf's Chancery under pressure.
guidance.disputed: Bartenstein thinks London will answer; Starhemberg, in his letter, counts only money already in a chest.
guidance.stakes: An ally in Conference who keeps careful accounts.
guidance.explain: A request to a foreign court goes through the Court Chancery; money from a guarantor would come as a subsidy or a loan raised in London, and slowly.

scene.title: The opinion on Silesia
scene.setting: Her Majesty's cabinet in the Hofburg, a little before noon. Your opinion lies open on the table, its margins marked. Count Starhemberg stands by the window with his hat under his arm.

lines.text: I read it twice. You do not fold three opinions into one; you write one and shout it. Good. Count Starhemberg, tell him what you told me.
That there is no money, Majesty, and that there will be some if you sign for it. The question is only what you sign away.

You put the case as you wrote it: the garrisons paid and filled now, the regiments in Moravia and Bohemia made ready, the money borrowed on Her Majesty's own name, from the town's bankers and from the allies who guaranteed her succession, before Berlin decides anything.
And if I borrow and nothing comes from Berlin, I have paid interest for a fright.
Eight in the hundred for a fright, Majesty. Cheaper than Silesia.

Then I will borrow. But I will not sign a bond I have not read. Count Starhemberg, bring me on Monday the terms, the houses and the revenue they want. Count Khevenhüller, bring me the regiments by name, how many men each has present and not on paper, and the road they take. The Conference sits on Monday and I will put it to them myself.
The President tells me the Council's opinions come to me through him. I told him that I asked for yours. If he holds your orders, I suppose you will tell me. Not before.
You bow. Starhemberg goes out with you as far as the guard-room and says nothing until the stairs.
She likes you because you are not afraid of her. Do not let her mistake it for being right.

commitments: You are to bring Her Majesty, by the Conference of Monday 31 October, the regiments for Silesia by name, their men present and their road.
Starhemberg is to bring Her Majesty the terms of credit, the houses and the revenue they want, by the same day.
Her Majesty will put men and money for Silesia to the Conference herself on 31 October.

undertakings.title: Credit for Silesia on Her Majesty's signature
undertakings.stage: Her Majesty will borrow; one banking house offers two to three hundred thousand florins in a fortnight, at eight in the hundred against a named revenue; Starhemberg would wait for the Estates.
undertakings.waiting: Starhemberg's terms on Monday and Her Majesty's choice of revenue.
undertakings.obstacle: Every revenue pledged to the bankers is lost to the Estates; the Chancery holds the door to London.

undertakings.title: The regiments made ready
undertakings.stage: Your orders that the regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary fill their ranks and stand ready to march lie unsigned in the President's chancery.
undertakings.waiting: The President's signature, or Her Majesty's resolution.
undertakings.obstacle: President Harrach, who will lay them before the Council first.

undertakings.stage: The steward has put the tailor off until Martinmas; the tailor's boy still calls.

calendar.what: The Conference: Her Majesty puts men and money for Silesia to it herself; your regiments and Starhemberg's terms due
The Lower Austrian Estates' homage; only then can they vote a grant

options.title: Borrow from the town's bankers now
options.objective: Two to three hundred thousand florins within the fortnight, on Her Majesty's signature.
options.reasoning: Money now pays the Silesian garrisons and the works before anything is decided in Berlin.
options.needs: Her Majesty's signature on the bond and a revenue named: Bohemian contribution, tobacco or salt.
options.risks: Eight in the hundred or more, six months; the revenue pledged is lost to the Estates; bad news raises the price at renewal.
options.ifWait: The offer stands only as long as the north is quiet.

guidance.suspected: The same houses already lend to the Hofkammer.

options.title: Wait for the Estates' grant and the Banco
options.objective: Cheaper money, raised in the proper way, after the homage.
options.reasoning: The Banco can advance against a voted grant at a lower rate and without selling a revenue.
options.needs: The homage done and the Lower Austrian Estates voting; weeks.
options.risks: Nothing for Silesia before December; the Estates name their price.
options.ifWait: This is the course of waiting.

guidance.known: The Banco's receipts for the year are assigned.
guidance.suspected: Starhemberg keeps the money in his own hands this way.

options.title: Call on the guarantor courts
options.objective: Subsidy or a loan raised in London and The Hague under the guarantee of the Sanction.
options.reasoning: A guarantee never called upon is a compliment; allies' money carries no interest and binds them to the cause.
options.needs: The Court Chancery to write; Sinzendorf's consent; weeks for any answer.
options.risks: Slow; Berlin will hear of it; the Chancery may let it sleep.
options.ifWait: London learns of the need only from others.

guidance.known: Britain guaranteed the Sanction by treaty in 1731.
guidance.disputed: Bartenstein expects an answer; Starhemberg counts only money in a chest.

debate.text: Name a revenue to a banker and you have sold it. Wait a month and the Estates will give it to you.
A month is time enough for Berlin to decide. Ask London today; it costs one letter.
I lend while the north is quiet. After that, I lend dearer.

staffBriefing.changed: Your opinion reached Her Majesty on the 26th, the President's copy the morning after. Her Majesty means to borrow and will put men and money to the Conference herself on Monday. The bankers offer money quickly and dearly; Starhemberg prefers the Estates; Bartenstein would call on the guarantors. The President holds your orders to the regiments until the Council sits.
staffBriefing.stakes: You have Her Majesty's ear and the President's grievance. If Monday's Conference goes your way, the war for Silesia is yours to prepare; if it fails, you went over the President's head for nothing.
staffBriefing.attention: By Monday: the regiments by name, men present and roads; which money to take; whether to ask Her Majesty to resolve the orders the President holds.

guidance.known: Wallis's returns from Glogau are expected about the 31st.
guidance.stakes: The figures you bring on Monday will be the ones the Conference argues over.

items.head: Vienna
items.text: The court mourning for His late Imperial and Catholic Majesty continues in all its rigour. Solemn exequies are held in the churches of the city, and the faithful attend in great numbers.

items.head: Vienna
items.text: Her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia has been graciously pleased to receive the condolences of several of the ministers of foreign courts, and to assure them of her friendship towards their sovereigns.

items.head: Vienna
items.text: The Lords of the Council of War, under His Excellency Count Harrach, continue to sit daily on the affairs of Her Majesty's armies.

items.head: From Berlin
items.text: Letters of the 15th report His Prussian Majesty at Rheinsberg, somewhat indisposed with a fever, the court quiet.

overheard.line: He borrows on her name before the Estates have sworn to it. Let him; the bond will carry his name too.

whereabouts.doing: Starhemberg called to Her Majesty's cabinet
in Her Majesty's cabinet, your opinion on the table
walking in the gallery, talking low

cast.name: Johann Georg Lenz
cast.office: Banker in the Wollzeile; lends to the court
cast.agenda: Lend to the Crown at a good rate against a revenue he can see collected; be first among the houses of the town.
cast.voice: Courteous, exact, a merchant's caution; names terms and never threatens.

hearsay.said: The Vice-President sends his papers to the Queen at night and to his President in the morning. In the Council they are counting the hours.
hearsay.source: your secretary, from the Hofkriegsrat chancery

hearsay.said: Khevenhüller wants a war in Silesia so that he may command it.
hearsay.source: your steward, from a lackey at the Chancery

dossier.note: Fact: read your opinion twice, means to borrow, and will put men and money to the Conference herself on 31 October; wants your regiments by name and Starhemberg's terms by then.
Fact: says the Banco can lend only after the Estates vote and warns against pledging Silesia's contribution; told you on the stairs not to let Her Majesty mistake courage for being right.

Fact: a banker in the Wollzeile, sounded by your secretary; offers with two other houses two to three hundred thousand florins at eight in the hundred against Her Majesty's signature and a named revenue.
Fact: holds your orders to the regiments unsigned until the Council sits, and says he will sign whatever Her Majesty signs. Report: was an hour with Sinzendorf on the 25th.
Fact: agrees with your conclusion, would call on the guarantor courts through the Chancery, and asks you to say so with him in Conference on Monday.
Fact: took your promise and asks for Sundays instead of dinners.

remarks: Her Majesty took the opinion as written and wants it proved by Monday. Plain figures opened the door; only plain figures will keep it open.
The President has found a form to stand behind. He will sign what Her Majesty signs, and remember who made her sign it.
Count Starhemberg is for us on the end and against us on the road. He wants the money to pass through the Banco.
Bartenstein offers his voice in Conference. He keeps accounts, and this time we are in credit.
The banker's offer is honest and dear, and good only while the north is quiet.

ledger.text: You told the Countess you regretted the dinner → she asks for Sundays instead.
Your opinion went to Her Majesty by your own hand: men and money now, on credit → the President had his copy next morning.
Orders to the regiments to fill their ranks and stand ready sent to the Hofkriegsrat → the President holds them for the Council.
A banker sounded → two to three hundred thousand florins at eight in the hundred against Her Majesty's signature and a named revenue.
Audience with Her Majesty and Starhemberg → she will borrow and put men and money to the Conference on 31 October; your regiments by name due then.

hidden.chronicle: Charles VI died 19–20 Oct 1740; Maria Theresa rules under the Sanction. Khevenhüller, Vice-President of the Hofkriegsrat, gave her plain Silesian figures before the first Conference (21 Oct): ~7,000 on the rolls, ~3,600 fit for the field, ~100,000 fl in the chest. The Conference notified the guarantors, told Wallis to repair and hold, fixed no money. Asked for his own opinion by the 27th, Khevenhüller sent it straight to the Queen on the evening of 26 Oct (copy to President Harrach next morning): men and money now, borrowed on her signature from Vienna's bankers and the guarantor allies. His draft Hofkriegsrat orders readying the regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary sit unsigned with Harrach, who will lay them before the Council and sign only what the Queen signs; Harrach and Sinzendorf met on the 25th and will argue for waiting. On 27 Oct the Queen, with Starhemberg, agreed to borrow in principle and will put men and money to the Conference herself on 31 Oct; Khevenhüller owes her the regiments by name and road, Starhemberg the terms. Options on money: banker Lenz (invented) with two houses offers 200–300,000 fl in a fortnight at 8%, six months, against a named revenue; Starhemberg prefers a Banco advance after the Lower Austrian homage and vote; Bartenstein would call on Britain and the States General under the guarantee via the Chancery, and backs Khevenhüller in Conference. At home the Countess asks for Sundays; the tailor still unpaid. Wallis's express reached Glogau early (25 Oct); his returns due ~29–31 Oct. Frederick learned of the death about 26 Oct and is consulting Podewils and Schwerin at Rheinsberg; Vienna knows nothing of it. Francis Stephen presses quietly for Neipperg's release. Unresolved: the money, the regiments, Harrach's grievance, Neipperg.

decisions.knows: Khevenhüller's opinion (men and money now, on credit); Starhemberg's empty chest; Harrach's claim that opinions come through him.
decisions.wants: To be obeyed and to hold Silesia, without signing what she has not read.
decisions.decides: Accepts borrowing in principle; demands terms from Starhemberg and regiments from Khevenhüller by 31 Oct; will put it to the Conference herself; leaves Harrach's hold on the orders for Khevenhüller to bring to her.

decisions.knows: The opinion went to the Queen before him; draft marching orders sit in his chancery.
decisions.wants: His primacy in the Hofkriegsrat; no open quarrel.
decisions.decides: Holds the orders for the Council; agrees with Sinzendorf to argue for waiting until the envoys report; will sign whatever the Queen signs.

decisions.knows: Envoy reports quiet; the notifications sent; Khevenhüller talks of borrowing from allies.
decisions.wants: No pretext for Berlin; the Chancery's monopoly on foreign business.
decisions.decides: Will argue in Conference that no regiment moves before Demeradt and the envoys report; any approach to London must be his and on his timing.

decisions.knows: The Banco's receipts assigned; the bankers' habits.
decisions.wants: No war without credit, the credit through the Banco.
decisions.decides: Supports men and money but advises waiting for the Estates; will bring the Queen honest terms on 31 Oct including Lenz's.

decisions.knows: Only what Khevenhüller's secretary asked and the town's talk of an empty chest.
decisions.wants: A good rate on a revenue he can see collected.
decisions.decides: Offers 200–300,000 fl with two other houses at 8%, six months, against the Queen's signature; terms to worsen on bad news.

decisions.knows: His cousin has said nothing for him; the Grand Duke is sympathetic.
decisions.decides: Writes again to Francis Stephen, offering his services against any enemy; Francis raises his release with Königsegg.

decisions.knows: Charles VI's death (about 26 Oct, at Rheinsberg); Austria's weakness by common report.
decisions.decides: Summons Podewils and Schwerin to Rheinsberg to consider his course (inference); no troops move yet.

fortune_used.outcome: Accepts borrowing in principle but will not sign or move troops before the Conference of 31 Oct.

fortune_used.for: Harrach's response to being passed over
fortune_used.outcome: Holds the regimental orders for the Council and coordinates with Sinzendorf.

fortune_used.for: The bankers' answer to the sounding
fortune_used.outcome: Will lend, but short and dear (8%, six months) against a named revenue.

fortune_used.for: Speed of the express to Glogau
fortune_used.outcome: Arrived on the 25th, a day early; Wallis's answer may come by the 29th.

canon: On 26 October 1740 Khevenhüller sent his written opinion on Silesia (men and money now, raised on credit) directly to Maria Theresa; President Harrach received a copy on the 27th.
Khevenhüller's draft Hofkriegsrat orders readying the regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary were held unsigned by President Harrach for the Council.
On 27 October 1740 Maria Theresa, with Starhemberg present, agreed to borrow in principle and said she would put men and money for Silesia to the Conference herself on 31 October.
Khevenhüller is to bring Maria Theresa the regiments for Silesia by name, men present and road, by 31 October 1740; Starhemberg the terms of credit.
Khevenhüller told his wife he regretted missing dinner; she asked for his Sundays instead.

dispatches.gist: He regretted missing dinner and will not let it happen again unless necessary.
The Vice-President asks what credit can be had for Silesia and on what security, and begs a word with him.
Without commitment: what would the house lend against Her Majesty's signature, how soon, on what terms.

The opinion on Silesia: pay and fill the garrisons, repair the works, ready the regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary; borrow on Her Majesty's signature from the town's bankers and call on the guarantor allies; act before Berlin decides.
Draft orders for signature: regiments in Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary to fill their ranks, draw arrears as money allows, and stand ready to march.
Copy of the opinion, for the President's information.

threads.note: Queen agrees to borrow in principle; Lenz offers 200–300,000 fl at 8% six months; Starhemberg to bring terms 31 Oct.
Bankers versus Banco-after-Estates versus guarantor subsidy; decision at the Conference of 31 Oct.
Francis presses Königsegg on Neipperg's release; Khevenhüller rising in the Queen's favour past Harrach and Sinzendorf.
Frederick learned of the death about 26 Oct and consults Podewils and Schwerin at Rheinsberg; no troop movement yet. Vienna knows nothing; Khevenhüller's men-and-money plan before the Conference.
Bartenstein proposes calling on Britain and the States General under the guarantee; depends on the Conference of 31 Oct and Sinzendorf.
Starhemberg would fund Silesia by a Banco advance against the grant voted after the homage.

starhemberg: 25 Oct 1740: asked him what credit could be had for Silesia.
